2.0.s.en: (1) David's charge to Solomon and the death of David

2.0.0.en: Before David died he gave his charge to his son Solomon, as fathers do when they feel that their departure from this world is near and give farewell counsels to their sons; and as Christ charged His disciples before His crucifixion and offered a farewell prayer (Jn 13-17). This charge includes a spiritual part (vv. 2-4) and an administrative part (vv. 5-9). David's purpose in these commandments is that his descendants hold to the commandments of God, so that they may secure God's care and remain firm on their thrones.

2.1.0.en: He told his son that he was on his way out of the earth, as every human being before him had departed, and charged him to be strong as a man to face the responsibilities of government, as Moses charged Joshua his disciple, who succeeded him in leading the people, to be strong (Deut 31:7, 23), because fear is the cause of all failure. Solomon's age at that time was about twenty years.

2.1.1.en: David's words show the calm of his soul and his acceptance of death as a natural matter for all humanity, which transfers him from the earth to a better life with God. Likewise his words "Be strong, and shew thyself a man" call Solomon to faith in God, so that he may become strong like a mature and capable man, because the power of God supports him and works in him.

2.2.0.en: Statutes: the law of God given to Moses.

2.2.2.en: Commandments: what is meant by them is the Ten Commandments.

2.2.3.en: Judgments: the laws found in the Law.

2.2.4.en: Testimonies: the sayings of God in general in His law.

2.2.5.en: David charged his son Solomon to hold fast to the commandments of God and His law which He gave to Moses, with all that it includes of teachings and spiritual worship, and to keep all of this so that he might prosper in his life. This charge resembles God's charge to Joshua after the death of Moses (Josh 1:7, 8). And so that Solomon might secure his people's submission to him, he must first obey the word of God himself.

2.2.6.en: If you want people to respect your words and esteem and obey you, then you must first become a disciple of the word of God in the Holy Bible, the teachings of the Church, and the guidance of your father of confession, so that you secure the soundness of your thought and its influence on those around you.

2.3.0.en: David reminded his son Solomon that if he held fast to the commandments and law of God, God would fulfill His promise that his descendants would reign forever (2 Sam 7:12-16). God's promise here includes two things:

2.3.1.en: 1- A promise conditional on keeping the commandments, by which God would establish the descendants of David on the throne of the kingdom; but they forsook the commandments of God, and the kingship was taken from them by the Babylonian captivity.

2.3.2.en: 2- An unconditional promise, which is King David's reign forever, and this is through Christ, who comes from the descendants of David. Even if they sinned and the kingdom came to an end and the captivity came, Christ would come and reign over the hearts of the believers forever, and the believers would become spiritual kings in Him.

2.3.3.en: What David means here is holding fast to the law of God and relying on Him, and not on military strength represented by a multitude of horses, or an alliance with Egypt, and likewise not multiplying marriages on the pretext of increasing offspring (Deut 17:16-20). But sadly Solomon fell into these errors, and God was angry with him.

2.4.0.en: Abner the son of Ner: the cousin of Saul and the commander of his army. He killed Asahel, Joab's brother, in self-defense, and Joab killed him treacherously in revenge for his brother Asahel.

2.4.1.en: Amasa the son of Jether: he was the son of Abigail, the sister of Zeruiah and of David, and therefore he was the son of Joab's maternal aunt. David appointed him commander of his army in place of Joab, who afterward met him and killed him treacherously with his sword in order to return to his position as commander of the army. That is, Joab acted treacherously and killed Abner and Amasa after they had been reconciled with David, and this is not considered an excuse even if it took place in time of war.

2.4.2.en: His girdle: what the soldier wears around his waist, hanging down.

2.4.3.en: After David finished his first, essential charge, he moved on to the judgments that Solomon had to carry out so that his kingdom might be secure. He began with Joab, for whom wisdom required choosing the right time to punish him, so that there would be no murmuring in the army, most of whose men admired their commander. David reminded his son Solomon of Joab's treachery toward both Abner the son of Ner and Amasa the son of Jether, since he shed their blood when they were innocent, which should not have happened, as they were not fighting against him. He dealt treacherously with them, for he pretended to embrace them, and while they were in his embrace he killed them, so that the blood flowed on his girdle and down to his sandals (2 Sam 3, 20). In this he resembles Judas the traitor who delivered Christ with a kiss. Joab was strong, indeed stronger than David, and often disobedient to him, so David could not punish him for killing Abner and Amasa until the right time came, when Solomon had become king and had another strong commander of the army, Jehoiada, and Joab deserved to receive his punishment for these two great crimes against God, David, and all the people, through the loss of two great leaders in war.

2.5.0.en: Joab did not make peace, so he cannot find peace for himself, and Solomon's reign, which is marked by peace and wisdom, cannot contain such persons. Therefore David charged Solomon not to let Joab's life end in peace, but to put him to death as the penalty for the crime he committed against innocent men. David had not killed him before, so that the kingdom would not be disturbed because of his chief role in leading the army, and to give him an opportunity to repent; but since he persisted and disobeyed the commandment of God and supported Adonijah to seize the kingship, he deserved to receive punishment for all his errors, and lest he try again to gain power over Solomon's kingdom. In this David is carrying out the law of God that requires the murderer to be put to death (Num 35:16); if he did not carry it out, David and Solomon would be condemned before God.

2.6.0.en: Barzillai: the head of a tribe living in Gilead east of the Jordan, who showed honor to David and those with him when he fled from the face of Absalom his son.

2.6.1.en: David moves on to speak of another person who did a special kindness for him and his army and showed courtesy when David was fleeing from Absalom. David wished to reward him in the person of his sons, so he charged Solomon to grant them the right to sit at the king's table because of the faithfulness and sincerity of their father, for Barzillai had excused himself from staying in Jerusalem with David because of his old age, and sent his son Chimham to accompany David (2 Sam 17:27-29; 19:31-39). To sit at the king's table means the greatest honor from the king and great trust on his part. From this we see David's justice, for he charges that wrongdoers be punished and that those who do good be rewarded.

2.7.0.en: Bahurim: a village near the Mount of Olives, that is, next to Jerusalem.

2.7.1.en: Mahanaim: a city east of the Jordan, north of the river Jabbok.

2.7.2.en: David mentioned a third person, Shimei the son of Gera the Benjamite, who had earlier shown intense hatred toward David and cursed him when he fled from his son Absalom. When David triumphed and returned to his kingdom, Shimei fell at his feet, pleading with him and asking for pardon and forgiveness, and David promised him that he would not kill him (2 Sam 16:5-8; 19:19-24).

2.8.0.en: Bring his hoar head down to the grave with blood: do not let him die a natural death, but kill him.

2.8.2.en: David asked his son Solomon not to hold Shimei guiltless, because he had sworn to him that he would not kill him, but that he should try him as a just judge and issue the judgment he deserved. For this Shimei was a deceitful man and not innocent, and if he were left alone he might plot against the kingdom and the king; that is, his apology to David was out of fear and not repentance, and therefore he could do harm to the kingdom. David does not mean a personal revenge here, but his punishment because he had sinned against the kingdom and against the Lord's anointed, King David; and David's promise to Shimei that he would not be killed was conditional on his obedience, so when he disobeyed King Solomon he deserved his punishment.

2.9.0.en: The city of David: that is, Mount Zion, which is part of the city of Jerusalem (2 Sam 5:7), where David placed the ark of the covenant of God.

2.9.1.en: David died and was buried on Mount Zion. The total period of David's reign was 40 years. The first capital of the kingdom was the city of Hebron, where he reigned for 7 years, and after he took the city of Jerusalem he moved the capital of his kingdom there, where he reigned 33 years. The custom in ancient times was to place tombs outside the cities, but Jerusalem was an exception to this, and the kings were buried in it, such as David and his descendants.

2.10.0.en: The kingship passed quietly from David to Solomon, and matters were settled, and he became ruler of the kingdom without rival. David had labored much in his wars with the surrounding nations until the kingdom became stable, and he handed it over to his son Solomon; indeed he also arranged for him the materials for building the Temple and provided him with much gold.

2.11.s.en: (2) Adonijah asks for Abishag as his wife

2.11.0.en: From this verse to the end of the chapter, the arrangements of God appear, which give Solomon an opportunity to be rid of the wicked who could oppose him in his kingship. It begins here with the coming of Adonijah, the elder brother of Solomon, who tried to seize the kingship against God's instruction that Solomon be made king, but Solomon forgave him after he became king and gave him an opportunity to repent and behave well. And now Adonijah comes to meet Bathsheba, Solomon's mother, and speaks kindly, declaring that he has come peaceably, because Bathsheba was surprised at his coming and suspected that he had an evil purpose. Adonijah politely asked to speak a word with her, and she gave him permission.

2.12.0.en: Adonijah claimed that he had every right of succession to the throne of the kingdom, as the eldest of David's living sons, and that all the people had been expecting this to be fulfilled, but the Lord, who has the right to set up whom He wills, chose Solomon. This is not a true acknowledgment of the will of God and submission to His will; rather he accepted it because he could not do otherwise. Though his words show submission to God and His will, he hid in his heart his resentment toward Solomon and his feeling that the kingship should have remained his, had it not been for God's intervention through David and the making of Solomon king. In appearance, then, he submits to the will of God, but in truth he rejects it.

2.13.0.en: Adonijah praised Bathsheba, saying that her words were heard by the king, in order to win her over so that she would agree to intercede with King Solomon, by virtue of her special familiarity with him, that he might allow him to take Abishag the Shunammite as his wife, the one who had been a nurse to his father David. This, of course, is a great error, because he dares to ask to marry his father's wife, thereby violating the Law. His request to marry Abishag means two things:

2.13.1.en: 1- His attraction to her beauty (ch. 1:4), that is, desire moved him toward her.

2.13.2.en: 2- It was the custom of pagan kings that the new king would take possession of all the property of the former king, even his wives and concubines. Perhaps Adonijah wanted, by marrying Abishag, to try to recover the kingship by taking the wife of the former king, David. This is what Absalom did before, by going in to his father's concubines to declare himself king in place of David (2 Sam 16:22). And Abishag, though she was only a nurse to David, was considered his wife, and it was not right for his son to marry her.

2.14.0.en: Bathsheba acted simply, and perhaps she did not understand Adonijah's evil intentions, or perhaps she felt that giving him Abishag would make him content and establish peace between him and his brother King Solomon, so she agreed to carry out his request and speak to Solomon.

2.15.0.en: When Bathsheba came in to her son King Solomon, he welcomed her and humbled himself greatly before her, for he rose from his throne and bowed down before her, and after this he honored her very much, as he seated her on a seat fitting her station at his right hand. This shows the extent of his love for his mother and his humility. It was a custom among the Jews, the Arabs, and the Greeks to honor the mother of the king by seating her at his right hand.

2.16.0.en: Bathsheba felt that her request was small and did not perceive its evil dimensions, so she asked her son King Solomon to grant her petition, and he welcomed her, waiting to hear the request.

2.17.0.en: Then she disclosed to him the request of his brother Adonijah, that Abishag the Shunammite be given to him as a wife.

2.18.0.en: With divine wisdom Solomon perceived Adonijah's evil intentions, so he answered his mother with disapproval to alert her to the seriousness of the request, for he said to her, "Why dost thou ask Abishag the Shunammite for Adonijah? ask for him the kingdom also." He declared Adonijah's evil, not only in breaking the law of God by asking to marry his father's wife, but also in his feeling that he was the eldest and deserving of the kingship. He revealed to his mother that Abiathar the high priest and Joab the commander of the army in the days of David were the ones who had planned this request with Adonijah, to seize the kingship again, as they had planned before.

2.18.1.en: Solomon's reply means complete rejection of this dangerous request. Despite his great honor for her and his humility before God, he leads his kingdom with wisdom and firmness, without flattery at the expense of the truth, even if it were to please his mother, for pleasing God is more important than everything. Solomon did not violate his promise to fulfill his mother's request, because he considered that the fulfillment of a promise must be within the bounds of the truth and the commandments of God (v. 20).

2.19.0.en: God do so to me, and more also: an oath meaning the necessity of carrying out what he says, otherwise God will punish him with the punishment he wishes to carry out on another, and even more than it.

2.19.1.en: If Solomon had forgiven Adonijah when he seized the kingship, now that Adonijah commits a great error like this - as we explained - he deserves death. Solomon asked Benaiah - who had become the commander of his armies - to carry out the sentence of death on Adonijah, who persisted in evil, and Adonijah was killed.

2.19.2.en: Beware of deceit and lying, for God is long-suffering, and in the end He will judge you to destruction, because you despised God and the others to whom you lied. Be content with what you have, keep away from desires, purify your heart from evil, and trust in the power of God, which will support you, so that you do not need this hateful lying.

2.20.s.en: (3) The expulsion of Abiathar from the priesthood

2.20.0.en: Anathoth: a city lying northwest of Jerusalem at a distance of four miles, and the birthplace of the prophet Jeremiah.

2.20.1.en: Solomon continued to cleanse his kingdom of his wicked opponents. After killing his brother Adonijah, he faced Abiathar the high priest, who had disobeyed the commandment of God by trying to seize the kingship for Adonijah, and thus deserved death. But in appreciation of Abiathar's labor in serving the ark of the covenant of God in the days of David (2 Sam 15:24-29), Solomon did not order him killed, but only removed him from the head of the priesthood, so that Zadok alone would remain high priest; for, as we mentioned, the headship of the priesthood in the days of David was shared by Zadok and Abiathar.

2.21.0.en: By the expulsion of Abiathar the word of God is fulfilled, that the descendants of Eli the priest be removed from the priesthood (1 Sam 2:30-33), for Abiathar was of the descendants of Eli the priest, and thus Zadok became the sole high priest, and he was of the descendants of Eleazar the son of Aaron.

2.21.1.en: Do not take part in sin and help another to evil, or plan for another the way of evil, lest you lose God's blessings in your life and are exposed to destruction. Be careful, and take care to please God before you please people.

2.22.s.en: (4) The killing of Joab and Shimei

2.22.0.en: The next person whose time had come to be called to account was Joab, who had allied himself with Adonijah in his rebellion, although he had previously stood on the side of King David against the rebellion of Absalom (2 Sam 18, 19). When the news reached Joab of Abiathar's expulsion from the priesthood, and he had already learned of what had happened to Adonijah when he asked for Abishag as a wife, he realized that his turn must come, so he fled to the altar of the Lord and laid hold on its horns.

2.23.0.en: Solomon had assigned someone to watch Joab's movements, because he knew his ability to overturn conditions given his former authority as commander of the army. So when they told Solomon that Joab was beside the altar, he sent Benaiah the son of Jehoiada and commanded him to kill Joab.

2.24.0.en: Benaiah went to carry out the order, but he did not wish to kill a person in a holy place, so he asked Joab to come out of the place, but he refused, insisting on staying beside the altar and holding its horns. Benaiah did not wish to kill Joab, who clung to the bronze altar, except after returning to Solomon.

2.25.0.en: The king ordered him to kill Joab where he was, before the altar, and reminded him of the judgment of the Law which says: "Thine eye shall not pity him, but thou shalt put away the guilt of innocent blood from Israel, that it may go well with thee" (Deut 19:13). Also, Joab's holding fast to the horns of the altar does not clear him of the innocent blood that he shed by killing both Abner the son of Ner and Amasa the son of Jether, since the Scripture says: "But if a man come presumptuously upon his neighbour, to slay him with guile; thou shalt take him from mine altar, that he may die" (Ex 21:14). But Solomon ordered that Joab be buried, in appreciation of his labor in leading the army throughout the days of David, and because he was also the son of Solomon's maternal aunt.

2.26.0.en: Upon the head of his seed: that is, the punishment will come upon the sons and grandsons of Joab if they walk in the evils of their father, as the second commandment makes clear (Ex 34). This was not revenge by Solomon for himself, but he ordered Joab to be killed in fulfillment of the commandment and of his father's instructions. Solomon also knew that in doing so he was fulfilling the word of Scripture: "Take away the wicked from before the king, and his throne shall be established in righteousness" (Prov 25:5). Solomon asks peace for the descendants of King David, meaning not only the throne of Solomon but all the descendants who would come from Solomon. And from the descendants of David comes Christ, who reigns forever, and He is the God of peace, who gives peace to those who believe in Him, over whose hearts He reigns, not in this age only but forever in the Kingdom of Heaven.

2.27.0.en: So went up: because the tabernacle was on a high place in Jerusalem.

2.27.1.en: Benaiah obeyed the king's command and went to Joab at the altar and killed him and buried him in his own land in the wilderness, where his house was, which carried with it some honor. He did not leave his body in shame and disgrace, because he had fought the wars of the Lord with King David, so he had this right to honor. The burial of a person in his house is a kind of honor, as happened with the prophet Samuel (1 Sam 25:1).

2.28.0.en: With the removal of Abiathar from the priesthood and the killing of Joab, two important positions in the order became vacant, which led Solomon to issue a decree appointing Benaiah the son of Jehoiada as commander of the army in the place of Joab, and appointing Zadok the priest in the place of Abiathar; that is, Zadok alone held the headship of the priesthood and Abiathar no longer shared it with him.

2.29.0.en: Because of Shimei the son of Gera's earlier bad conduct toward the kingdom, Solomon summoned him from his town Bahurim and sentenced him to live in Jerusalem under restriction, so that he would be under his close watch and not plan anything against the king, for Shimei was a chief of the tribe of Benjamin, and if he returned to his tribe he could plot against the king.

2.30.0.en: The brook Kidron: a valley that extends 2.5 km northwest of Jerusalem to the southeast of it. It lies between the wall of the city on its western side and the Mount of Olives on the eastern side, and extends to the Dead Sea.

2.30.1.en: Solomon warned Shimei that if he went beyond the boundaries of the city, he would have sentenced himself to death. Therefore he must not leave the city under any circumstances, or he would be put to death.

2.31.0.en: Shimei pledged to obey the king's command and remained for a long time living in Jerusalem, not leaving it.

2.32.0.en: Gath: one of the five great Philistine cities, lying on the coast of the Mediterranean Sea southwest of Jerusalem.

2.32.1.en: After three years had passed in this state, two servants of Shimei ran away and took refuge with Achish the son of Maachah, king of Gath. Shimei sent people to search for them everywhere, and they found them there in Gath.

2.33.0.en: When Shimei learned that his two servants were in Gath, he hurried himself and brought them from there, forgetting his pledge to King Solomon not to leave Jerusalem, or making light of the king's command, or perhaps thinking that the king would not discover his leaving Jerusalem.

2.34.0.en: Solomon learned that Shimei had gone out of Jerusalem and gone to Gath and returned again to Jerusalem.

2.35.0.en: Solomon summoned Shimei and reminded him of his former oath, that he would not go out of Jerusalem or be put to death. Solomon asked him why he had broken his oath and violated the commandment which he had charged him with.

2.36.0.en: Then Solomon declared the reasons for the sentence on Shimei, namely that he was fully aware of the evil that lay in his heart toward his father David, ever since he cursed him and threw stones at him, and now the Lord returns his evil upon his own head. As for David and his descendants, they receive a blessing, and the throne of David is established before the Lord forever.

2.37.0.en: Solomon commanded Benaiah the son of Jehoiada to kill Shimei, and he did so.

2.37.1.en: Thus, by getting rid of those who formed a danger to the continuance of Solomon's reign, namely Adonijah, Abiathar, Joab, and Shimei, peace and stability prevailed in the kingdom, and Solomon was able to control matters without rival.

2.37.2.en: Be careful in carrying out your promises to God, and obey His commandments also, and you will secure your peace, and even your blessed eternity. Do not be negligent, adding new sins to your sins.
